question: Did the CIDOC CRM SIG add a way to qualify group membership by role (for example, distinguishing a 'master' from an 'apprentice' within a group) through new sub-properties of group membership, and how was that decided?
gold_answer: Christian-Emil Ore raised the problem that E74 Group could express symmetric relations (e.g. siblings sharing membership of a family) but had no clean way to express asymmetric roles like master/client; Stephen Stead proposed adding role-qualifying sub-properties (P107.1 and P144.1, 'kind of member'), and he and Ore drafted full scope notes and examples ready for a vote. Once circulated, however, Martin reported a negative vote arguing the existing Group/subgroup mechanism (treating each role-holder as a singleton subgroup) already covered the case without any extension, which Ore called 'artificial'. The debate that followed turned on whether membership roles are best seen as 'offices' (a structural feature of the Group itself) or as relational sub-properties, and never reached a stated conclusion on whether to adopt P107.1/P144.1; it drifted instead into a related but separate fix — whether to drop the Group scope note's requirement of 'two or more members' — and the archive in this period records no final decision on the original proposal either way.
key_facts: The trigger was an asymmetric relation (e.g. master/client) that E74 Group's symmetric-membership model could not express directly
Stephen Stead and Christian-Emil Ore drafted P107.1 and P144.1 ('kind of member') qualifiers with full scope notes, intending to bring them to a vote
Martin reported a negative vote proposing singleton subgroups as an alternative to the new properties, which Christian-Emil Ore called 'artificial'
No final decision adopting or rejecting P107.1/P144.1 appears in the discussion; it shifted instead into debating whether to drop the 'two or more members' requirement in the Group scope note
produced_answer: Yes. In November 2008 Christian-Emil Ore raised the problem that P107 'has current or former member' cannot express asymmetric roles within a group (his example: master vs. apprentice, or 'associate member' vs. 'full member'). Stephen Stead proposed adding a P107.1 sub-property ('in the role of'); Martin Doerr agreed it would let CRM express subtleties of group structure elegantly, noting roles can change after joining so P107.1 can't simply be inferred from the type of the Joining event. Christian-Emil Ore then drafted the actual property text, naming it 'P107.1 kind of member' (tentative name) and a parallel 'P144.1 kind of member' on P144 (the fuller path via E85 Joining), with a royal-family example ('Prince Phillip, kind of member: husband'). This was put to an e-mail vote on 2008-11-14 as part of the CRM v4.3 -> v5.0 change set and was approved (Stephen Stead and Christian-Emil Ore both voted 'Approved subject to edits'). A negative vote then arrived (relayed by Martin on 2008-11-20) arguing the same effect could be achieved without a new sub-property, by modeling master/apprentice as singleton sub-groups whose type expresses the role. Christian-Emil Ore rejected this as too artificial/indirect ('like epicycle models of the planet orbits') and pointed out CRM has no sub-group property to support it; Martin was open to the idea but did not force the vote, and said the P107.1/P144.1 addition would stand as accepted if no further votes came in by the following Monday. No further opposing votes are visible in the archive, and the property (documented today as P107.1 'kind of member', usable to specify 'the type of membership or the role the member has in the group') is present in the current CIDOC CRM standard, confirming the sub-property was adopted.

question: Did the CIDOC CRM SIG ever commit to a comprehensive list of disjoint class pairs (classes that can never share a common instance) for the benefit of OWL-style implementations, and if not, what was the reasoning for not doing so?
gold_answer: No — the SIG explicitly and repeatedly declined to produce a comprehensive list of disjoint classes, judging such a list of doubtful practical value and likely to conflict with keeping the standard's class definitions concise. The published guidance confirms only two genuinely fundamental disjoint pairs (Temporal Entity vs. Persistent Item, and Physical Thing vs. Conceptual Object); an earlier effort toward a fuller list was abandoned, with the recommendation on record being to give up on formal disjointness declarations altogether. The stated reasoning was that most other candidate disjoint pairs have real counter-examples in practice — for instance, a single uninterrupted repair act that is simultaneously a removal and an addition of a part, or real linked-data mappings that deliberately model one node as both an Actor and a Collection — so a blanket list would misrepresent how the classes are actually used; the suggested path forward was to evaluate proposed disjoint pairs individually, case by case, with supporting use cases, rather than adopt any general list.
key_facts: Only two disjoint class pairs are confirmed as fundamental in the published guidance: Temporal Entity/Persistent Item and Physical Thing/Conceptual Object
An earlier attempt at a fuller disjointness list was abandoned, with the recorded recommendation being to abandon formal disjoint class declarations altogether

The reasoning given was that most other candidate disjoint pairs have genuine counter-examples in practice (e.g. a single repair event that is both a part removal and a part addition, or real mappings that overload one node as both an Actor and a Collection)
The suggested resolution mechanism was case-by-case evaluation of individually proposed disjoint pairs with use cases, not a comprehensive standing list
produced_answer: No. The CIDOC CRM SIG explicitly declined to publish a comprehensive list of disjoint class pairs. In thread t0590 (Nov 2011, 'Implementation recommendation for disjointness'), Martin Scholz (Erlangen CRM) pointed out that the CRM standard's 'Disjointness' section states a comprehensive declaration of all disjoint class combinations 'has not been provided here; it would be of questionable practical utility, and may easily become inconsistent with the goal of providing a concise definition,' and that ISSUE 92 concluded the SIG 'should abandon the idea of disjoint class declarations altogether.' Martin Doerr confirmed this directly, saying 'In the past the CRM-SIG team gave up to define a comprehensive list of disjoint classes, because there were too many exceptions.' He named only two fundamental, uncontroversial disjoint pairs (E2 Temporal Entity/E77 Persistent Item, and E18 Physical Thing/E28 Conceptual Object), plus Time-Span/Place/Dimension as obvious but not worth stating. Beyond that, he explained many candidate pairs are only 'likely' or context-dependent disjoint (e.g. a Physical Feature vs. the Place it occupies, or getting rid of Time-Spans in practice) or are genuinely combinable in a true ontological sense (e.g. destruction and activity, Image and Linguistic Object). For events especially, he said it is 'very difficult to state any useful disjointness' since that would require excluding any possible immediate interaction between event types and separating their participants and space-time volumes -- illustrated with an example of removing and re-adding a chair leg being either one event or two depending on interpretation. Aldo Gangemi separately suggested disjointness axioms, if added, be kept in an optional pluggable module rather than the core ontology, precisely because they cause problems when CRM is aligned with other ontologies for unforeseen uses. This position was raised again unresolved in 2019 (thread t1247) when a user asked the same question about a comprehensive disjointness list.

question: CIDOC CRM has a shortcut property letting a physical object 'depict' something directly, bypassing the conceptual image or inscription it carries. Was a parallel proposal to add equivalent shortcuts for physical objects that merely 'refer to' or are 'about' something (rather than depict it) accepted by the SIG?
gold_answer: No resolution is recorded. A member proposed adding physical-domain siblings of the existing depiction shortcut, so a physical object could state a 'refers to' or 'is about' relationship directly instead of first creating an empty conceptual node just to carry that property. Several members supplied real-world examples meant to establish practice (CRM's usual bar for adding constructs): a gravestone epitaph, a blue plaque referring to both a person and a building, and a museum drawing whose documentation names a play and its scriptwriter. Two members initially argued that in every example the 'aboutness' really belongs to an intermediate conceptual object (such as an inscription) being carried by the physical object, so no new shortcut was needed; the proposer countered that this same argument, if valid, would equally invalidate the existing depiction shortcut, so it could not be used selectively against the new proposal. Martin Doerr laid out CRM's general principle that shortcuts over information-bearing intermediate objects are usually avoided because they can work against information integration, but acknowledged the examples were new evidence CRM-SIG would need to take up at a future meeting. The thread ends with the proposer asking whether the issue had even been logged on the CRM issues list, and no reply on the matter appears in the record - the proposal was left open, neither accepted nor rejected.
key_facts: A member proposed new physical-domain shortcut properties, siblings of the existing 'depicts' shortcut, to avoid creating an empty conceptual node just to carry a 'refers to'/'is about' statement

Two other members argued the 'aboutness' in the examples given (gravestone epitaph, blue plaque, museum drawing referencing a scriptwriter) belongs to an intermediate conceptual object carried by the physical object, not the physical object itself
Martin Doerr said the examples counted as new evidence that CRM-SIG would need to take up at a future meeting, per CRM's practice-based justification principle
The thread ends with no confirmation that the proposal was logged, accepted, or rejected
produced_answer: No. In thread t0630 ("ISSUE: P62 needs a parent and a sibling", started 2012-07-05 by Vladimir Alexiev), Alexiev proposed adding P67a_refers_to and P129a_is_about as physical-domain sibling shortcuts to P62_depicts, parallel to the conceptual-domain P67/P129, based on British Museum data examples (e.g. a drawing of an actress whose data also names the scriptwriter, a blue plaque referring to a person and a building). Several examples were offered (Matthew Stiff, Sebastian Rahtz), but Stephen Stead argued these were really conceptual objects (inscriptions) carried by the physical object, not direct physical 'aboutness'. Martin Doerr gave a detailed justification for why CRM generally avoids such shortcuts for inscriptions (to preserve the identity/integration role of the intermediate text-bearing object), while saying CRM-SIG would need to consider the new evidence at a future meeting. The thread ends on 2012-07-20 with Alexiev asking whether it had been logged as an issue, and no acceptance is recorded. The current CIDOC CRM standard (v7.1.3) confirms no such properties were ever added: P67 and P129 still have domain E89 Propositional Object only, and P62 remains the sole physical-object 'aboutness' shortcut - so the parallel proposal was not accepted.

question: Did the SIG ever settle the question of whether a CIDOC CRM shortcut property (like a direct 'produced by' link) logically implies the existence of the fuller event-based path it stands in for?
gold_answer: No, the archive shows this was left an open disagreement rather than a settled position. Martin Doerr, working with Carlo Meghini on a first-order-logic formalization of the CRM, argued from a pure-logic standpoint that if a longpath can be inferred, its intermediate nodes logically exist, independent of whether they are ever materialized in a database. Vladimir Alexiev pushed back hard, arguing shortcuts should never entail long-paths in practice: the intermediate node isn't unique, inferring it produces unlocatable 'Skolem' blank nodes that cause problems when integrating richer data later, and by a YAGNI-style principle nothing should be inferred that isn't needed. Christian-Emil Ore and Detlev Balzer largely sided with Doerr's logic-first framing, but the thread ends with Vladimir asking Doerr to clarify his 'soft' versus 'strict' classification of shortcuts, and no reply or resolution appears in the archive.
key_facts: Martin Doerr argued that if a shortcut's underlying longpath can logically be inferred, its intermediate nodes logically exist, treating this as a question of logic separate from database/knowledge-base practice.

Vladimir Alexiev opposed inferring long-paths from shortcuts, citing non-unique intermediates, OWL-inferred blank ('Skolem') nodes that can't be matched during later data integration, and the YAGNI principle.
The thread ends with Vladimir asking Doerr to explain a 'soft' vs. 'strict' classification of shortcuts, and no answer or resolution is recorded.
produced_answer: Not settled with a single universal yes/no. Martin Doerr opened ISSUE 'Shortcut semantics' in Aug 2014 (thread t0780), noting that while the full event path always implies the shortcut, only in a few cases (e.g. 'rights held by') does the shortcut logically imply the intermediate path exists. Vladimir Alexiev argued a shortcut should never infer a long path (Skolemization/YAGNI concerns); Doerr, Detlev Balzer and Christian-Emil Ore argued the intermediate node's existence can be logically inferred even if not materialized. No consensus was reached in that thread. As homework, Ore then produced a classification (May 2015, thread t0855) sorting individual shortcuts into 'strong' (shortcut implies the full path/intermediate node exists, e.g. P105 right held by, P56 bears feature, P107 has current or former member, P49-P52 keeper/owner) versus 'weak' (does not imply it, e.g. P53/P55 location, P59 has section, P152 has parent) -- explicitly noting the classification depends on 'ontological commitment', i.e. it is property-specific, not a single rule. The SIG kept revisiting this for years: in the Oct 2019 homework for ISSUE 357 (thread t1268), Ore adopted the pragmatic simplification of 'defining all shortcuts as weak' in the formal FOL spec text, and in Nov 2019 (ISSUE 420, thread t1287) stated 'in general, we don't describe the CRM shortcuts as strong', treating strong shortcuts as rare exceptions found case by case. The topic resurfaced again in 2022 under ISSUE 613 ('weak inverse shortcuts'), where the group found even that term 'opaque'/'problematic'. So the SIG never closed this with one general logical rule -- they settled instead on a per-property, case-by-case classification (strong vs weak) that was still being refined a decade later.

question: Over the course of a year, the SIG repeatedly discussed what CIDOC CRM's class for rights actually represents -- the abstract legal concept of a right, or a specific instance of someone holding a right over an object for a bounded period -- along with how to handle joint or partial ownership shares. Did the SIG ever settle on a single answer?
gold_answer: No -- the archive shows this was never resolved. One member repeatedly pressed the SIG on whether the Right class denotes the concept of a right (which, as a Conceptual Object, cannot simply cease to exist just because its legal validity lapses) or the concrete holding of a right by a specific actor over a specific object for a limited time, and the two readings kept producing contradictory answers about things like the end of an ownership right after resale. Two members separately floated adding a new property or class to capture the period during which a right is actually in force, distinct from the right's existence as a concept, but this stayed an unadopted suggestion rather than an agreed change. The senior modeller's final word was that 'right' is simply an ambiguous natural-language term with multiple legitimate senses, that modelling joint or fractional ownership and the legal domain generally was too complex to settle by email, and that a dedicated working group would need to be restarted -- noting that an earlier such effort had already stalled once its partner organization withdrew. No resumption of that group, nor any scope-note change or new property, appears in the archive for this period.
key_facts: Whether the Right class (E30) denotes the abstract legal concept or a concrete, time-bounded holding of a right was never formally resolved -- no scope-note change or SIG vote is recorded in this period.

A proposal to add a new property or class capturing a right's period of legal validity, separate from its existence as a concept, was raised by more than one member but remained an unadopted suggestion.
The discussion also raised joint/partial ownership (e.g. two parties each holding a percentage share of a right) as unresolved, with no modelling solution agreed.

The senior modeller proposed restarting a dedicated rights-modelling working group, noting a prior effort had already stalled after a partner organization withdrew; no such group is shown reconvening.
produced_answer: No, the SIG never settled on a single answer. In the 'Rights model' thread (t0972, Feb-Mar 2017), Robert Sanderson raised the question of whether E30 Right is the abstract right/content of a right, or the instance of holding it, and Martin Doerr replied that there are really three distinct things -- the holding of the right, the content of the right, and the concept of the right -- and that whether holding can be merged with content 'is to be discussed.' The joint/partial ownership question (e.g., two people each owning 50% of an object, via P148_has_component) was raised in the same thread but Martin called it 'horribly complicated,' said the CRM was not built for such business-transaction modeling, and proposed splitting it off into a separate extension effort ('CRM social') rather than resolving it in CRM core. A related proposal for a new 'Right Holding' class with temporal properties (thread t0976) was submitted as an issue but not adopted. The follow-up thread 'End of Existence for Rights?' (t1019, Aug-Sep 2017) revisited the same abstract-concept-vs-instance dilemma; Martin's final reply there says a Right 'can be both' senses depending on context, suggests renaming E30 to something like 'Right Terms' and improving the scope note, but no e-vote or scope-note change is recorded closing the issue. The archive's own chronology for E30 marks both the 2017-02-28 and 2017-08-14 episodes as 'unresolved.'

question: The community considered adding a property to let two instances of the general Type class be ranked relative to each other (for example, to say a condition-report value like 'Good' outranks 'Average'). Did the group settle on this property, and if so, in what final form?
gold_answer: No, this was never settled. The idea was raised in January 2019 as a new property on E55 Type, and its proposed name changed repeatedly during discussion: first 'is conceptually greater than', then 'conceptually follows/precedes', then a suggestion of 'ranked higher than/ranked lower than'. Martin Doerr repeatedly questioned, on methodological grounds, whether such a property belonged in CRM base at all rather than being left to SKOS's existing broader/narrower relation or its OrderedCollection mechanism, and this scope question was never resolved. By June 2019 the property (again called 'is conceptually greater than') had been shifted out of CRM base into the CRMsci extension, with homework assigned to add concept-scheme context to its scope note, but the discussion ends with Martin raising further open mathematical questions about whether the relation is a partial or total order and how transitivity and part-of relations interact with it. No vote was ever taken.
key_facts: The proposed ranking property for E55 Type went through several candidate names ('is conceptually greater than', 'conceptually follows/precedes', 'ranked higher than/lower than', then back to 'is conceptually greater than')
Martin Doerr repeatedly questioned whether the property belonged in CRM base versus being left to SKOS, and this was never resolved

By mid-2019 the property had been moved from CRM base to the CRMsci extension, but no vote adopted it and open questions about its precise mathematical nature (partial vs. total order) remained unanswered
produced_answer: Yes, the group settled on it, though only provisionally within the 2018-2019 window and it kept being revisited afterward. Stephen Stead raised the issue in thread t1156 ('**NEW ISSUE** Ordinal Property for E55 Type', Jan 2019), motivated exactly by the condition-report example in the question (Excellent/Good/Average/Poor/Critical) plus map scales and fire hazard ratings, proposing 'Pxx is conceptually greater than (is conceptually less than)', domain and range E55 Type, many-to-many, transitive. A long naming debate followed -- alternatives floated included 'conceptually follows/precedes' (Franco Niccolucci, then adopted by Stead mid-thread), 'ranked higher than/ranked lower than' (Stead again, backed by Robert Sanderson), 'is_ordinal_superior_to/inferior_of' (George Bruseker), and 'ordinally after/before' (Athanasios Velios) -- alongside a substantive dispute (mainly from Martin Doerr) over whether this belonged in CRMbase at all versus CRMsci or being left to SKOS. Thread t1156 ends in Jan 2019 unresolved, with Doerr proposing to move it into CRMsci and Christian-Emil Ore still questioning the whole approach. Resolution came at the CRM-SIG meeting in Paris: in thread t1219 ('Issue 407: Ordinal Property for E55 Type', June 2019) Robert Sanderson reports 'Agreement at Paris SIG that this could go into CRMsci and thus "Oxx is conceptually greater than"', with a revised scope note adding concept-scheme/vocabulary context (e.g. 'good' and 'average' in the same conservation-report vocabulary). So the final form settled on in 2018-2019 was: property (is conceptually greater than / is conceptually less than), domain and range E55 Type, transitive, placed in CRMsci rather than CRMbase. A later 2022 thread (t1631) and the current ontology lookup show this became CRMsci property O28, still described there as 'a draft property' with Martin Doerr raising fresh scope concerns (whether it should apply to E55 Type generally or be restricted to a new subclass) -- so full closure of the issue extended beyond 2019, but the name/placement settled in the Paris SIG agreement is what stuck.

question: The community discussed extending the CRM so that non-human animals (for example, a bird building a nest) could be documented as having carried out an activity, the way a human actor would. Did the SIG settle on a new class structure for this, and if not, what was left unresolved?
gold_answer: No, the SIG did not settle on or adopt any new class structure for non-human actors, despite substantial discussion. The case was raised using the example of a bird (or dinosaur) building a nest, for which the model had no adequate way to assign agency short of a weak 'occurred in the presence of' relation. Two members sketched a detailed proposal for a monotonic extension, introducing a sibling superclass to the human-actor class with parallel individual and collective biological-agent subclasses, and suggested eventually renaming the existing human-specific classes accordingly. However, another member consistently held that any such extension needed an established community documentation practice and willing domain experts first, neither of which existed yet, and separately drew a firm line that machines or robots should never count as actors regardless of their apparent agency, since they act on behalf of human instructions much like a trap does. A librarian on the list added that an analogous 'animal as agent' idea had already been proposed and rejected in the bibliographic (FRBR/LRM) community for similar reasons. The discussion ended with a proposal to document the debate itself as methodological material and the sharing of a real-world animal-tracking use case, but no class or property was ever adopted.
key_facts: No new class or property for non-human actors was adopted; the discussion ended without the SIG reaching a decision
A detailed extension proposal was put forward (a sibling agent superclass with individual/collective biological-agent subclasses, and renaming existing human-actor classes), but it was not adopted

One member's stated position was that such an extension requires an established documentation practice and domain experts first, which the group had not yet found, and that machines/robots should never count as actors
A librarian noted that an analogous animal-as-agent proposal had already been considered and rejected in the FRBR/LRM bibliographic model for similar reasons
produced_answer: No, the SIG did not settle on a new class structure. The topic ('New Issue: Non-human Actors', started by Robert Sanderson on 2021-09-21, using exactly the bird-building-a-nest example) was discussed through mid/late November 2021 but ended without agreement. Martin Doerr supported adding non-human (specifically living, biological) actors in principle, suggesting they belong in CRMsci as a sibling generalization to human actors, but insisted the SIG first needed real documented use-case data tracing individuals and domain (biology) experts before committing to new classes - he stated the reason animal actors were never modeled was precisely the lack of an experts group to consult. George Bruseker and Robert Sanderson produced a concrete draft class sketch (a new top class 'Agent' generalizing E39 Actor and a new sibling 'Biological Agent' branch, with parallel Individual Agent/Collective Agent and Individual Biological Agent/Collective Biological Agent classes, and renaming E39/E21/E74 to 'Human Agent'/'Human Person' accordingly), but this was only a discussion proposal, not adopted. Left unresolved: (1) whether/how to formally define 'individuality' and 'collectivity' for animals across the animal kingdom, (2) whether machines/robots/software should be treated similarly (Martin argued machines are not actors, just reactive instruments akin to traps, a separate modeling problem), (3) the cost/benefit and recall-precision methodological questions Martin posed about whether 'P12 occurred in the presence of' plus text is already sufficient versus needing new 'done by'-type properties/classes, and (4) finding biology/natural-history domain experts to validate the model. The thread's last message (2021-11-19) is just Martin sharing a background PowerPoint example of CRM-compatible animal tracking 'for future discussion' - no decision was recorded.

question: CIDOC CRM's RDF implementation has long included a combined class for a name that is also treated as an expression in a particular language (formed by multiple inheritance from the classes for linguistic objects and for appellations), but this class exists only in the RDF files, without a documented scope note in the base standard. Did the SIG ever agree to formally add this class, with a proper scope note, to the standard itself?
gold_answer: No, and the archive never settles this. A 2022 thread pointed out that the RDF-only class for a name-that-is-also-a-linguistic-expression is inconsistently labelled and has no documentation outside the RDFS file, and proposed promoting it to a fully specified class in CRMbase. This produced an extended and ultimately unresolved debate: Martin Doerr held that CRM's minimality principle bars adding classes that contribute nothing beyond what multiple inheritance already implies, and repeatedly asked for a scope note and disambiguating examples showing that 'the language of a name' is a well-defined, non-arbitrary notion, raising counterexamples about transliterated and multi-language names that were never fully answered. Robert Sanderson and George Bruseker countered that the class is ubiquitously used in practice and that the minimality principle is already applied inconsistently to other classes (their example was E27 Site), so it should simply be documented rather than left informal. Francesco Beretta proposed reframing the concept instead as a kind of 'appellation in a language' activity/state class, which Rob argued did not meet the original requirement. The discussion carried into a formal issue at the following SIG meeting, but by the last messages in this exchange Martin was still preparing the disambiguating examples he considered necessary, and no scope note, wording, or vote had been agreed.
key_facts: The disputed class is the RDF-only combined class for a name expressed in a language (linked via the property for language of expression), which has no scope note or agreed single name in the base CRM standard, only inconsistent labels in the RDFS file.

Martin Doerr's objection rests on CRM's minimality principle (no class from multiple inheritance alone without its own distinguishing properties), and his repeated request for disambiguating examples of 'the language of a name' was never resolved.

Robert Sanderson and George Bruseker argued the class is already in wide practical use and that the minimality principle is applied inconsistently elsewhere (their counterexample was E27 Site), so it should be documented rather than left informal.

Francesco Beretta's alternative proposal to model it as an 'appellation in a language' activity/state class was rejected by Rob as not meeting the stated requirement, and the thread ends with no scope note, wording, or vote agreed.
produced_answer: No. The class is E33_E41_Linguistic_Appellation, a multiple-instantiation class of E33 Linguistic Object and E41 Appellation used for names in a particular language, which existed only in the RDFS (with even an inconsistent naming, E33_E41 vs E41_E33) and never had a scope note in the base standard. George Bruseker raised this in thread t1649 (Nov 2022, 'error in RDFS for 7.1.1...') and formally opened it as Issue 624 ('Add E33_E41_Linguistic_Appellation to the Official Specification', thread t1655), with Robert Sanderson also supporting adding it. Homework was produced (thread t1682) proposing alternatives (a new P.. property, LRM Nomen, Francesco Beretta's sdh:C11 'Appellation in a Language'), but Martin Doerr and others objected that no adequate scope note/semantics had been agreed (what exactly makes an Appellation 'language-specific', instance-specific vs universal use, etc.). The thread ends in Dec 2022 with Martin still working on a clarifying counter-example and no consensus reached. No later e-vote, decision, or closure of Issue 624 was found anywhere in the archive through Jan 2026 (the latest indexed messages). So the SIG discussed but never agreed to formally add this class with a scope note to CIDOC CRM Base -- it remains RDFS-only and the issue appears to still be open/unresolved.
